stories.title: East Coast Project Phase 4 Launched at Île Aurore (Seychelles)

publications.text:
HERM­INIE LAUNCHES EAST COAST MEGA-PROJECT: DEVELOPMENT AMBITION MEETS POLITICAL OPPORTUNITY FOR UNITED SEYCHELLES

By Seychelles Pulse News | 12 October 2026

ÎLE AURORE, MAHÉ President Dr Patrick Herminie has officially launched the East Coast Project Phase 4 (ECP4), marking a major milestone in Seychelles’ long-running land reclamation programme and placing housing, economic development and the country’s limited land resources firmly on the national agenda.

The launch ceremony, held at Île Aurore on 9 October, brought together senior government officials, Vice-President Sébastien Pillay, representatives of Belgian dredging company Jan De Nul and other invited guests. The project will create new land at Île Aurore and Providence, opening opportunities for residential, industrial, tourism and infrastructure development.

A PROJECT WITH NATIONAL CONSEQUENCES

The proposed reclamation covers approximately 55 hectares according to the State House announcement, with other reports giving a slightly higher estimate. Government plans envisage more than 1,800 houses, alongside schools, sports facilities, industrial areas and other developments. These are future development ambitions, not completed achievements.

For a country where mountainous terrain and limited coastal land constrain housing and business expansion, the project addresses a significant development challenge. Its ultimate value, however, will depend on whether the newly created land translates into affordable housing, productive investment, employment and infrastructure that Seychellois people can access.

President Herminie presented the initiative as an investment in future generations, emphasising the need to balance development with environmental responsibility. 

THE POLITICAL SIGNIFICANCE FOR UNITED SEYCHELLES

Beyond its engineering and economic dimensions, the launch carries political significance for President Herminie and the United Seychelles (US) party. Major infrastructure projects can become defining features of an administration’s public identity, particularly when they address issues that directly affect households and businesses.

1. Demonstrating a governing agenda

The project gives the administration a visible, long-term development initiative to communicate to the public. Housing shortages, access to land and the cost of development are concerns with direct consequences for families. By placing these issues at the centre of a national project, Herminie can demonstrate that his government has identified tangible development priorities.

For United Seychelles, this creates an opportunity to explain its governing programme through a concrete infrastructure initiative rather than relying solely on political speeches or party messaging.

1. Connecting national development with household aspirations

The promise of homes, schools, roads and business opportunities has considerable public relevance. If the project ultimately delivers these benefits fairly and efficiently, the administration will have a measurable basis on which to demonstrate progress.

For the party, the political opportunity lies in connecting national investment to improvements in everyday life. But the distinction between a promise and a delivered benefit will remain crucial.

1. Building a long-term development narrative

Land reclamation is not new to Seychelles. Earlier phases of the East Coast Project helped create areas subsequently used for housing, industry and essential infrastructure. ECP4 therefore builds on a development programme that predates the current administration.

Herminie’s political challenge and opportunity is to show how the fourth phase will respond to today’s needs and what additional value it will deliver. United Seychelles can highlight the launch as part of the government’s development agenda while recognising the historical foundations of the wider programme.

1. Engaging young people and future homeowners

The project has particular relevance for younger Seychellois who aspire to own homes, establish businesses and raise families. The President explicitly framed the initiative around the needs of future generations.

This provides the government with an opportunity to explain how land availability, housing policy, skills development and employment are connected. For United Seychelles, the strongest evidence of progress would be accessible opportunities for young people, rather than the scale of the ceremony itself.

1. Attracting investment and supporting economic diversification

The government has identified industrial land, marina facilities, tourism and residential development as potential uses for the reclaimed areas. Properly planned investment could expand economic activity and create employment opportunities.

Politically, this allows the administration to present infrastructure development as part of a wider economic strategy. The benefits will depend on investment actually materialising, jobs reaching Seychellois workers, and public interests being protected in the allocation and development of land.

THE ACCOUNTABILITY TEST: PROMISES MUST BECOME RESULTS

Despite the project’s potential, its launch should not be confused with its completion. The public will ultimately need clear answers on project costs, financing, implementation schedules, environmental safeguards and the criteria governing the allocation of reclaimed land.

Questions about who benefits from future residential and commercial developments will be especially important. If public land creates substantial private investment opportunities, the government will need to demonstrate that the wider Seychellois population also receives a fair share of the economic and social benefits.

Environmental monitoring will be equally significant. Reclamation can create new development space, but coastal ecosystems and marine resources must be protected through effective safeguards and transparent oversight.

These are not merely technical matters. They will shape public confidence in the administration and influence how the project is judged over time.

CONCLUSION: A POLITICAL OPPORTUNITY, NOT A GUARANTEED VICTORY

President Herminie’s launch of East Coast Project Phase 4 gives his administration and United Seychelles a significant national development initiative around which to communicate their priorities. Housing, land availability, employment and investment are issues that reach beyond party politics and affect the country’s long-term future.

The political advantage for United Seychelles will depend on what happens after the launch: whether construction proceeds as planned, whether costs are managed responsibly, whether land is allocated transparently and whether the promised opportunities reach ordinary Seychellois.

For now, the project represents an important step in the government’s development programme. Its lasting political and national significance will be determined not by the ceremony, but by the results delivered to the people of Seychelles.

publications.text:
President Herminie Emphasises Monetary Stability as New Central Bank Governor Prepares to Take Office

Maintaining monetary and financial stability remains a key priority for Seychelles, President Dr Patrick Herminie emphasised during a meeting with the newly appointed Governor of the Central Bank of Seychelles (CBS), Ms Sarah Lloyd, at State House on Wednesday afternoon.

The President formally presented Ms Lloyd with her letter of appointment ahead of her assuming office on 1 November 2026.

During their discussions, the importance of maintaining a stable financial environment and the Central Bank's role in safeguarding the country's economy were highlighted. The meeting also placed particular emphasis on the institution's responsibility to preserve price stability and sustain confidence in the financial system.

Having already undertaken a preliminary visit and held discussions with the Central Bank team, Ms Lloyd expressed confidence in the institution's capabilities and looked forward to serving the country in her new role.

President Herminie underscored the importance of continuity in the Central Bank's work as Ms Lloyd prepares to assume leadership of the institution. He wished her success in carrying out her responsibilities.

Speaking to the press following the meeting, Ms Lloyd outlined her priorities, placing particular emphasis on further developing the financial services sector while preserving financial and price stability.

“Alongside the already established priorities of the institution, my focus will be on further deepening the financial services sector, while ensuring that we preserve the stability of our financial system and maintain price stability,” she said.

Addressing questions about the independence of the Central Bank, particularly in situations where its policy direction may differ from that of government, Ms Lloyd stressed the importance of protecting the institution's autonomy and maintaining its longstanding reputation for integrity.

She acknowledged that differences in policy direction could arise but noted that constructive engagement and mutual understanding would be essential in navigating such situations.

“The Central Bank of Seychelles has a history and legacy of being a strong institution that has always delivered with integrity and independence. Continuing to maintain that reputation will be paramount in fulfilling my duties,” she stated.

Ms Lloyd further explained that stakeholder engagement would play an important role in fostering a shared understanding of policy decisions, even where differences exist between the Central Bank and government.

She noted that greater appreciation of the reasons behind differing policy positions could help both institutions identify common ground, particularly as they ultimately work towards the same broader economic objectives.

However, she maintained that the independence of the Central Bank as an institution must remain protected.

Turning to her immediate priorities upon assuming office, Ms Lloyd said her first task would be to engage with staff across the institution to better understand their needs and how they could continue working together to deliver the Central Bank's services effectively.

“I think, as with any new role, my first priority will be to engage with all the staff and take an introductory approach to understanding their needs, ensuring that I know exactly what they require going forward and how we can continue working together,” she explained.

Reflecting on her decision to accept the appointment, Ms Lloyd described her return to the Central Bank as a particularly meaningful moment in her professional career.

Having begun her career at the institution in 2007, she spent approximately 12 years serving in various capacities before moving into commercial banking.

“Although I subsequently moved into commercial banking, accepting this role really felt like coming home,” she said, describing the Central Bank as the institution where she began a career of which she remains proud.

Ms Lloyd brings extensive experience in banking, financial risk management and economic research. Prior to her appointment, she served as Chief Risk Officer of Absa Bank Zambia PLC, a position she had held since March 2022. She previously occupied the same position at Absa Bank (Seychelles) Limited between February 2019 and March 2022.

Her career at the Central Bank began as a Research Assistant before she progressed to Economist and later Senior Financial Stability Analyst. During her tenure, she established and managed the Financial Stability Unit and represented Seychelles at regional and international forums.

She holds a Master of Science in Financial Economics from City University London and a Bachelor of Science in Banking and International Finance from Cass Business School.

Her appointment comes as the Central Bank continues its mandate of safeguarding monetary and financial stability, with Ms Lloyd identifying institutional independence and further development of the financial services sector among her priorities.

Safeguarding the independence of the Central Bank of Seychelles (CBS) will remain a central priority under its new leadership, Ms Sarah Lloyd emphasised following her meeting with President Dr Patrick Herminie at State House on Wednesday afternoon.

The President formally presented Ms Lloyd with her letter of appointment, highlighting the important role of the Central Bank in safeguarding the country's economy and maintaining public confidence in the financial system.

Ms Lloyd, who brings extensive experience in banking and financial risk management, will officially assume office on 1 November 2026.

The President wished her success as she prepares to take on her new responsibilities.

stories.title: Compassion Question Raised Over Ramkalawan's Leadership
stories.description: A Facebook post published on 25 October 2026 addressed former president Wavel Ramkalawan and questioned whether Seychelles would be safe under his leadership again. Referring to reactions celebrating President Herminie (Patrick Herminie)'s hospitalisation and wishing him death, the author raised concern about compassion in political leadership; the post does not say Ramkalawan endorsed those reactions.

publications.text:
🇸🇨 SEYCHELLES, THINK! A MESSAGE TO THE FORMER PRESIDENT.
With all due respect, Mr Former President Wavel Ramkalawan, Seychelles had a choice, and you had your chance for the past five years. The people made their decision, and that choice deserves to be respected.

As a young Seychelloise woman in my 30s, I know our current government is not perfect. When they are wrong, we must speak up and hold them accountable. But beyond politics, where is our humanity?

When President Herminie was hospitalised, the reactions celebrating his illness and wishing him death deeply disturbed me. Before he is a President, he is a human being, a father, and someone's loved one.

Do we really want a leader who fails to remind supporters that compassion must come before politics? Do we want a nation where political differences make us celebrate another person's suffering?

Perhaps God allows certain situations to happen so we can reflect on the kind of country we truly want.

My fellow Seychellois, we can disagree politically without losing our humanity. No government is perfect, but leadership must come with compassion, humility, and respect for human life.

Mr Former President, you had your chance. Today, my concern is whether Seychelles would be safe in your hands again if compassion is missing from the leadership we witness.

Seychelles, think carefully. What kind of example are we setting for our children?

❤️ Let us choose humanity over hatred, compassion over cruelty, and unity over division.

🇸🇨 God bless Seychelles!

stories.title: Fire Destroys One Home at PMC Emergency Housing
stories.description: The Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency reported that a residential fire at the PMC Emergency Housing block in Barbarons (Seychelles) destroyed one unit and partially damaged two adjoining units; no injuries were reported. The report was published on 28 October 2026, but the incident date is not specified; the cause remains undetermined, and the Agency and Seychelles Police have initiated an investigation.

publications.text:
Residential Fire Incident at PMC Emergency Housing, Barbarons.🔥🚒 

The Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency (SFRSA) wish to inform of a residential fire incident that occurred at the PMC Emergency Housing block at Babarons.
 
At approximately 08:45 hrs, the Victoria Fire Station received a report of a residential fire outbreak at Babarons. The incident was immediately relayed to the Anse Royale Fire Station for response. 

Two fire tenders from Anse Royale Fire Station, manned by a total of six (6) firefighters, were dispatched to the scene. A backup fire tender from Victoria Fire Station, manned by four (4) firefighters, was subsequently mobilized to provide additional support. Fire crews arrived on scene approximately 20 minutes after the initial call was received. 

Upon arrival, firefighters observed that one residential unit within a single storey block of houses was fully engulfed in flames, with the fire posing an immediate threat to two adjacent units located on each side of the affected structure. 

Following a rapid assessment of the situation, firefighting operations commenced immediately to contain and extinguish the fire while preventing further spread to the neighbouring units. 

The fire was brought under control within approximately 15 minutes of firefighting operations, and complete extinguishment was achieved after approximately 40 minutes of continuous firefighting efforts. 

The affected building is of concrete block construction and covered with corrugated iron sheet roof. As a result of the incident, one residential unit was completely destroyed, while two adjoining units sustained partial fire damage. 

Fortunately, no injuries were reported in connection with the incident.

The cause of the fire has not yet been determined. An investigation has been initiated by the Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency, in collaboration with the Seychelles Police Force, to establish the origin and circumstances surrounding the fire. 

The Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency would like to remind the public of the importance of maintaining and practising good fire safety and housekeeping, and remaining vigilant to potential fire hazards within the home. 

Terence Arnephy(Mr.) 
Divisional Officer 
Public Relations Officer

publications.title: Who Knew First? Four Mercenary Coups Foreign Governments Saw Coming
publications.text:
In March 2004, a Boeing 727 carrying 64 men landed in Harare to collect weapons for a coup in Equatorial Guinea. Five weeks earlier, the British government had received an intelligence report about a possible coup there. It never told Equatorial Guinea.

It was not the first time. Over nearly thirty years, small private armies tried to seize four African countries, and each time it later emerged that a foreign government knew more than it said at the time. This documentary follows the evidence case by case to ask a precise question: who knew first, and what did they do with what they knew?

THE FOUR CASES
• Benin, 1977: a dawn attack on Cotonou, and a case of operation papers left on the runway, examined by a UN Security Council mission.
• Seychelles, 1981: Mike Hoare's "Froth-Blowers", a gun battle at Mahé airport, and South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
• Comoros, 1995: Bob Denard's last coup, France's Operation Azalée, and a 2006 Paris judgment about what French intelligence knew.
• Equatorial Guinea, 2004: Simon Mann, the "Wonga Coup", and a British minister's written statement to Parliament.

We separate what was admitted on the record, what official bodies found, and what is still only alleged. Knowing about a coup is not the same as ordering one, and the four cases show very different degrees of involvement.

This channel investigates foreign involvement in modern African history through archival records, testimony, official findings and carefully attributed allegations. If evidence-led history is your kind of documentary, consider subscribing.

President Herminie Receives Final Report of the Board of Inquiry on the Importation of Firearms

The President of the Republic, Dr. Patrick Herminie, this morning received the final report of the Board of Inquiry on the Importation of Firearms at State House. The report was presented by the Chairperson of the Board, Honourable Justice Duncan Gaswaga.

Also present were the Members of the Board, Mrs. Nissa Thomson, Mr. Justin Dogley and Mr. Edward Annacoura; the Secretary to the Board, Ms. Kyra Arnephy; and the Chief of Staff in the Office of the President, Ms. Jenifer Vel.

The Board was established on 31 December 2025 by President Herminie, in his capacity as Commander-in-Chief of the Defence Forces, under the Defence (Board of Inquiry on Importation of Firearms) Regulations, 2025 (S.I. 103 of 2025). Its members were sworn in at State House on 19 January 2026. All proceedings of the Board were held in camera.

The inquiry examined who authorised and financed these importations, how the firearms and ammunition were stored, and whether any unregistered armouries remain in existence.

Speaking to members of the press after the handover, Justice Gaswaga shared some of the recommendations contained in the report. He said that, if fully read, internalised and implemented, the recommendations would bring significant change to how things are done, including in matters of national security.

The recommendations address how operations involving the armed forces should be conducted, and how arms are issued and used, with clear procedures to be put in place for such operations. They also set out general standards for officers of the Seychelles Defence Forces and the Police who carry weapons.

The Board further recommended that the country develop a modern armoury, together with proper systems governing how weapons are stored, moved, regulated and disposed of.

In receiving the report, President Herminie thanked the Chairperson and Members of the Board for their work. The President will now study the report and its recommendations in detail. stories.title: SBC Criticized for Not Questioning President's Absence
stories.description: A Facebook publication dated 21 October 2026 criticizes the Seychelles Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) for not asking the Minister of Foreign Affairs why the President was absent when the minister read the President’s speech on 19 October, or why the President addressed the public by message rather than in person about bad weather on 20 October. The author says the broadcasts showed a lack of journalistic curiosity and describes SBC as reactive state media, leaving the public without answers about the President’s absence.

publications.text:
There is still no news of the President this morning. This post is not about him. We will sooner or later find out why he was not seen in public for a few days and why he missed several key engagements. 

This post is about our national broadcaster, SBC. The lack of curiosity demonstrated by the SBC in the whereabouts of the President recently is staggering. Two nights ago the news reported on the opening of the meeting of ambassadors and honorary consuls. The SBC showed the  Minister of Foreign Affairs reading the speech of the President. The journalist then interviewed the Minister. This was a perfect opportunity to ask the Minister why the President had not appeared to read his own speech. The journalist didn't. Why? 

Then, last evening, SBC read out a message from the President addressing the bad weather which had struck the country. Again, not a word about why the President was sending a message and not addressing the people in person. All it would have taken to clear the issue was a short message to State House.

We deserve more from our national broadcaster. Journalists must be inquisitive and proactive. We seem to have slipped back into a reactive state media, where the news is controlled by the government and the public is ignored.

When the SBC Act was passed by the Assembly recently, the Opposition members warned that this would happen. It has taken only 2 months for us to have been proved right. Whether this is deliberate or as a result of self-censorship by journalists is not important. The result is the same. The population is left in the dark and the darkness will only get worse.

#AnseAuxPins has become the first district in Seychelles to officially launch the Seychelles Community Recycling Initiatives, marking an important step towards strengthening waste separation and recycling at community level.

 The initiative, which was officially launched this week, introduces dedicated sorting bins where residents can bring selected recyclable materials for collection and onward processing by local recyclers.

The aim is to recover valuable materials, reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill, and make recycling more accessible to communities.

- 🍾 Glass drinking bottles

It is supported by local recycling partners: Metaluco, Brikole, Precious Plastic and DeRecycler, who play an important role in ensuring that collected materials can be recovered and put to further use.

🌱 A shared responsibility

The launch of SCRI in Anse Aux Pins is a starting point for bringing recycling closer to residents and encouraging more responsible waste-management practices. Its success will depend on community participation and the proper separation of recyclable materials.
Residents are encouraged to make use of the facility and help keep valuable resources out of our landfill.

stories.title: Industry Minister (Geralda Desaubin) Acknowledges Shortcomings, Sets Priorities
stories.description: In an address published on 6 November 2026, the Minister for Industry and Enterprise (Geralda Desaubin) marked one year in office by acknowledging unmet expectations and continuing difficulties for businesses and entrepreneurs in Seychelles. She set priorities for her second year, including strengthening local production, supporting entrepreneurs, and improving accountability and performance within the Ministry and its agencies.

publications.text:
ONE YEAR IN OFFICE.
REFLECTING ON THE JOURNEY, TAKING RESPONSIBILITY AND MOVING FORWARD

Address by Ms. Geralda Desaubin, Minister for Industry and Enterprise

Good Day All,

Today marks one year since I took the oath of office as the Minister for Industry and Enterprise. One year. Twelve months of responsibility, challenges, decisions, opportunities, lessons and above all, service to our country.

Today, I do not want to simply celebrate an anniversary or present a list of achievements. I want to take this opportunity to reflect honestly on the journey so far, acknowledge where we have made progress, recognise where we could have done better and share my vision and determination for the road ahead.

When I assumed this responsibility, I understood that I was taking on a Ministry with an important mandate. Industry and enterprise are not simply about businesses, factories, products or statistics. They are about people. They are about livelihoods, employment, opportunities, innovation and the economic future of Seychelles.

Every small business represents someone's dream. Every local manufacturer represents an opportunity to create value within our country. Every entrepreneur who takes a risk represents the courage and determination that we need to build a stronger economy. And that is the responsibility I accepted.

Over the past year, we have worked to strengthen the visibility and recognition of Seychelles-made products, promote our local businesses and create greater opportunities for our entrepreneurs. Through initiatives such as Seychelles Made, we have continued to champion local production and encourage our people to appreciate, support and take pride in products made in Seychelles.

Our participation in international platforms, including the China International Import Expo, is part of that ambition. We want Seychelles to be recognised not only as a beautiful tourism destination, but also as a country capable of producing quality products, developing innovative enterprises and contributing meaningfully to international trade.

These are important steps. But I want to make one thing very clear. I do not measure success simply by the number of meetings we attend, the events we organise, the photographs we take or the international platforms we participate in. Real success must be measured by the difference we make in people's lives and in the performance of our businesses.

Are our businesses growing? Are we creating more opportunities for local producers? Are we making it easier for entrepreneurs to establish and expand their businesses? Are we becoming more competitive? Are we creating employment? Are our local products reaching new markets? These are the questions that must guide our work.

And this brings me to the other side of leadership. Acknowledging what has not gone as well as we would have wanted.

I will not stand before you today and pretend that everything has been perfect. It has not. There are expectations that we have not yet met. There are initiatives that have taken longer than anticipated. There are businesses that continue to face difficulties, entrepreneurs who feel that they need more support and challenges within our business environment that still require urgent attention. There are areas where we could have moved faster, communicated better and delivered more effectively. I acknowledge that.

I do not see acknowledging our shortcomings as a weakness. I see it as an essential part of responsible leadership.

We must be honest with ourselves if we genuinely want to improve. We cannot continue doing things simply because that is how they have always been done. We must be prepared to question existing practices, challenge inefficiencies, make difficult decisions and embrace new ways of working. I also recognise that government cannot solve every challenge overnight. But that must never become an excuse for inaction or a reason to lower our expectations. Our people expect results, and rightly so. Our entrepreneurs do not simply want to hear about policies. They want to experience the benefits of those policies. They want an enabling environment, timely support, access to opportunities and practical solutions to the challenges they face. And we must remain focused on delivering these.

As I begin my second year in office, my message is simple. We must move from promises to performance, from planning to implementation and from activities to measurable results.

My priorities moving forward are clear.

First, we must strengthen local production. Seychelles cannot continue to depend so heavily on imported goods without making a determined effort to develop the productive capacity we have at home. We may not be able to produce everything, but we can certainly do more with the resources, skills and talent available to us.

Second, we must empower our local entrepreneurs. Our small businesses must not be treated as an afterthought. They are an essential part of our economy. We must create an environment in which they can grow, innovate, access markets and become more competitive.

Third, we must strengthen the Seychelles Made initiative. I want us to see more genuine Seychelles-made products, greater recognition of our local producers and more opportunities for these products to reach regional and international markets.

Fourth, we must encourage investment, innovation and technology. We need to modernise our industries, improve productivity, embrace sustainable production and attract partnerships that bring real value to Seychelles.

Fifth, we must invest in our people. Our young people must see entrepreneurship and industrial development as real opportunities for their future. We must encourage them to think creatively, develop their skills, take calculated risks and become job creators rather than only job seekers.

And finally, we must strengthen accountability and performance within our Ministry and agencies. Every institution under this Ministry must understand its responsibility, deliver on its mandate and demonstrate the results expected of it. I expect commitment, professionalism, urgency and accountability.

To our business community, I want you to know that you matter. Your concerns matter. Your challenges matter. Your ideas matter. You are not simply recipients of government support, you are partners in building our economy. I encourage you to continue engaging with us, challenging us constructively and sharing your ideas. But I also encourage you to believe in your own potential. Do not underestimate what a Seychellois business can achieve. We must stop looking at the size of our country as a limitation and start recognising the opportunities that exist beyond our borders.

To our manufacturers, producers, entrepreneurs and businesswomen and businessmen, I want to see you grow. I want to see you become more ambitious. I want to see you compete internationally and proudly represent Seychelles.

To the staff of the Ministry and our agencies, I thank you for your work throughout this first year. But let me also say this: our second year must demand even more from us. We must work together, communicate better, take ownership of our responsibilities and remain focused on delivering for the people we serve.

I also want to make a personal commitment. I will continue to listen, even when the feedback is difficult. I will continue to engage, even when the discussions are uncomfortable. I will continue to make decisions in the best interest of the sector and our country, even when those decisions are not always popular. I will not claim to have all the answers, but I will remain committed to finding solutions. I will not promise that every challenge will disappear, but I will promise that we will continue working to address them. And I will not pretend that the journey will always be easy, because meaningful development requires patience, courage, consistency and determination.

One year in office has taught me that leadership is not about having all the answers. It is about having the courage to confront the questions, the humility to learn from mistakes and the determination to keep moving forward. I am proud of the progress we have made, but I am equally conscious of the work that remains.

I do not want to be remembered for simply occupying a ministerial office. I want our work to leave a meaningful and lasting impact on the development of Seychelles. I want us to build an Industry and Enterprise sector that creates opportunities, strengthens livelihoods, encourages innovation and contributes to a more diversified and resilient economy.

So today, I celebrate the journey, acknowledge the lessons, take responsibility for the shortcomings and renew my commitment to the work ahead.

To everyone who has supported us, challenged us, encouraged us and walked alongside us during this first year, thank you. We may not have achieved everything we set out to do, but we have an opportunity to do more, to do better and to deliver stronger results.

One year down. The work is far from finished. The next chapter must be defined not by what we say, but by what we deliver. Let us move forward with renewed energy, greater ambition, stronger collaboration and commitment to Seychelles.

Thank you, and may God continue to bless Seychelles🇸🇨

stories.title: Seychelles Seeks Grenada's Support for Venn's Town (Seychelles) Bid
stories.description: The Seychelles Times reported on 2 November 2026 that Seychelles was seeking Grenada's support for the Venn's Town (Seychelles) World Heritage bid. It said Seychelles' Minister for Foreign Affairs and the Diaspora (Barry Faure) met Grenada's Minister of Tourism, Creative Economy and Culture (Senator Adrian Thomas) on the margins of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda; the meeting date and any outcome are unspecified.

publications.text:
Seychelles and Grenada Discuss Strengthening Bilateral Cooperation

Minister for Foreign Affairs and the Diaspora, Mr Barry Faure, met with Grenada’s Minister of Tourism, Creative Economy and Culture, Senator Adrian Thomas, on the margins of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) 2026 being held in Antigua and Barbuda.

The discussions focused on the importance of strengthening solidarity and cooperation among Small Island Developing States (SIDS), particularly in promoting cultural heritage. The Ministers exchanged views on the common vulnerabilities faced by their respective countries including their dependence on exports and tourism and the impact of external shocks and geopolitical developments on tourism flows.

During the meeting, Minister Faure sought Grenada’s support for Seychelles’ efforts to secure UNESCO World Heritage recognition for Venn’s Town, an important national historical site and tourist attraction. He highlighted the site's significant cultural and ecological value to Seychelles, noting that its recognition would complement the country’s two existing UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Aldabra Atoll and Vallée de Mai, located on Praslin Island.

stories.title: Bel Ombre (Seychelles) Tourism Plan Faces Coastal Development Criticism
stories.description: A Facebook publication dated 1 November 2026 criticises the Bel Ombre (Seychelles) tourism master plan, prepared by the Ministry of Housing and Lands, arguing that its strategic environmental assessment (SEA) comes too late to reconsider core land-use choices. The plan covers about 90 arpents and proposes three hotel sites totaling more than 53 arpents, while reserving a public beach of under 10 arpents; the publication raises concerns about coastal habitats, public access and the assessment’s independence.

publications.text:
Bel Ombre : trois nouveaux hôtels, mais quelle vision du territoire ?

À ce rythme, ne restera-t-il bientôt que la plage publique située à côté du village de Bel Ombre comme dernier espace littoral véritablement accessible à tous dans cette partie de l’île ?

Le nouveau Master Plan touristique de Bel Ombre, préparé par le ministère du Logement et des Terres, concerne environ 90 arpents de terres de l’État, entre la limite est de l’hôtel SO Sofitel et la rivière Jacotet. Il comprend 58 arpents de terres de l’État non engagées et 32 arpents de Pas Géométriques et de Land Settlement Land, dont la déproclamation et le transfert vers le ministère du Logement et des Terres sont envisagés pour permettre la réalisation du plan. Quelque 38 planteurs sont également concernés par ces terres.

Après exclusion d’environ 16 arpents pour les reculs et autres contraintes, le plan porte sur quelque 74 arpents. Il prévoit trois sites hôteliers totalisant plus de 53 arpents, deux parcelles destinées à des activités touristiques, identifiées sur le plan comme des villas ou appartements, une parcelle commerciale, des parkings et une plage publique de moins de 10 arpents dans la zone la plus instable et humide. 

Il faut saluer la décision du ministère de l’Environnement de soumettre l’ensemble de ce Master Plan à une Évaluation Environnementale Stratégique (SEA), conformément à l’Environment Act 2024. C’est une avancée importante : plutôt que d’évaluer les impacts d’un hôtel après l’autre, il s’agit enfin d’examiner les conséquences d’un plan d’aménagement dans son ensemble. Les termes de référence prévoient notamment l’analyse des impacts cumulés, l’identification des zones sensibles et la comparaison de plusieurs scénarios, y compris celui de ne rien construire.

Mais pourquoi faut-il attendre qu’un plan prévoyant une telle artificialisation soit déjà élaboré pour se poser ces questions fondamentales ? Cette SEA donne quelque peu le sentiment d’un rattrapage de dernière minute. Une évaluation stratégique devrait précisément intervenir en amont, avant que les grandes orientations foncières et touristiques ne soient posées.

D’autant que les termes de référence reconnaissent eux-mêmes la vulnérabilité du site : dunes et plage de Beau Champ classées zone écologiquement sensible, zones humides, drains naturels, risques d’inondation liés à la rivière Jacotet et terrains situés à moins de deux mètres au-dessus du niveau de la mer. Le site se trouve également dans la zone de transition de la Réserve de biosphère UNESCO des Gorges de la Rivière Noire–Bel Ombre. Selon les projections du BRGM, le recul du trait de côte pourrait atteindre, selon les secteurs, entre 10 et 70 mètres d’ici 2100.

Pourquoi, face à de telles réalités, l’artificialisation reste-t-elle notre point de départ ? Le site est notamment considéré comme adapté au tourisme parce que des hôtels et des infrastructures existent déjà à proximité. Mais depuis quand le fait d’avoir déjà construit justifie-t-il de construire davantage ? C’est précisément cette logique d’accumulation qui nous a conduits à la situation actuelle.

Et surtout, où cette logique s’arrêtera-t-elle ? Le Master Plan concerne une portion bien délimitée, entre le SO Sofitel et la rivière Jacotet. Mais qu’en sera-t-il des autres espaces encore non construits, notamment de la portion littorale située de l’autre côté du SO Sofitel, vers les établissements hôteliers existants ? Allons-nous progressivement voir ces dernières parcelles attribuées, les unes après les autres, pour de nouveaux hôtels, des villas ou d’autres développements immobiliers ? À quel moment déciderons-nous que certains espaces doivent tout simplement rester libres de toute construction ?

Autre rappel : Le dossier KPMM, toujours à Bel Ombre, devrait également nous interpeller. Un bail avait été accordé pour un projet hôtelier sous l'ancien régime qui n’a jamais vu le jour, avec des arriérés(non paiement du bail) qui dépasseraient 43 millions de roupies. Le ministre du Logement et des Terres avait évoqué plusieurs options, dont la résiliation ou la reprise du bail. Le Premier ministre avait lui-même qualifié ce dossier de « den of corruption and mismanagement ». Où en sommes-nous aujourd’hui ? Si ces terres sont reprises, quelle sera leur destination ? Seront-elles enfin réexaminées dans une perspective d’intérêt public, ou simplement proposées à un autre promoteur ? Ce dossier illustre précisément pourquoi nous devons repenser notre politique d’attribution et de gestion des terres publiques sur le littoral.

Nous saluons donc la SEA, mais elle doit pouvoir remettre en question les orientations mêmes du Master Plan, et non simplement chercher à en atténuer les impacts. Elle doit examiner de véritables alternatives : conservation des espaces naturels, restauration des dunes et des zones humides, espaces publics, activités communautaires et tourisme moins intensif, tout en tenant compte des planteurs et des habitants qui utilisent déjà ces terres.

Il faut également tirer les leçons du passé. Des plans d’aménagement et des allocations foncières ont déjà avancé sans véritable évaluation stratégique d’ensemble. Si notre politique d’aménagement reste fondée sur toujours plus de constructions, qu’est-ce qui empêchera demain de revenir à des allocations de parcelles au coup par coup, sans Master Plan et sans évaluation des impacts cumulés ? Une telle approche reviendrait à fragmenter les décisions pour éviter de poser la question essentielle : quelle capacité notre littoral a-t-il encore à accueillir de nouveaux développements ?

Enfin, les termes de référence indiquent que le financement de la SEA devrait être assuré par les promoteurs potentiels. Il faudra neanmoins rester vigilant sur les questions d'indépendance de l’évaluation et la transparence du processus devront être pleinement garanties meme si ministère de l’Environnement en conserve le pilotage.

La question dépasse donc largement ces 90 arpents. C’est l’avenir de tout le littoral de Bel Ombre, et au delà qui mérite d’être pensé dans son ensemble. Pourquoi continuer à envisager de nouvelles affectations foncières sans avoir défini une vision cohérente de ce qui doit être protégé, restauré, partagé ou éventuellement aménagé ?

Une SEA ne doit pas servir à justifier des choix déjà envisagés, mais à déterminer si ces choix sont réellement souhaitables. Et peut-être est-il temps d’admettre que, sur certaines des dernières portions non construites de notre littoral, le meilleur projet d’aménagement est précisément de ne pas construire.
